You have done your duty. It is honest and comes from the heart—it will reward you well—for you deserve it. You have so manifested your practical assent to the whole and important political truth, that a virtuous and upright public magistrate shall not be without his reward in the estimation of the community. You have expressed your sense of the excellent administration of our state Government for the past year in the only real manner, in which the public sense can be expressed—by an increased majority of suffrage in support of those whom it approves.

A tribute to the benevolent and pious philanthropy is included in the result. You have also given two federal Senators to the Senate of this Commonwealth—men of worth and principle, of honour and integrity. May such ever grace the character of those, whom the people elect to honour. And while federalism may not always be an object of public confidence, it will never fail to flourish. FEDERALISM is the cause of the country—and never let that cause cease to be cherished in Massachusetts. Whatever may be its fortune in other sections of the union—however it may rise and fall—there its genuine principles are less under blight and the precepts of Washington less faithfully observed, here let federalism ever find its HOME. Let Massachusetts, ever continue to be the HEAD QUARTERS of sound principles and pure practices—and her friends in this state be always ready to rally round her standard. Upon the maintenance of the federal cause in all its purity, depend, under heaven, the happiness and well-being of this country. While its principles are regarded, its effects will be perceived. And if America be ever again destined to attain the proud and insensible height she once enjoyed, her prosperity will be found to be essentially united with faithful adherence to that policy pursued in the days of Washington, of which federalism is only the proper name. Democracy, so far as it is anti-federalism, is a miserable shortsighted policy, which pursues the contemplated good of party at the expense of the interests of the country, and only aspires to the possession of present power at the peril of future prosperity; and such it will be found upon experience. This nation—of which Washington was the father and founder, and in which federalism still remains as leaven—has made a perfect trial of all things, it will then hold fast to that which is good—and federalism will finally be found to be the true political secret of national honour, strength and virtue. Let every Federalist then maintain his integrity. Let him be sensible that the success of federalism depends in tact upon himself. Let him be faithful to the principles he has adopted. BOSTON, July 7.

By the Brig Sally Barker, arriving at this port from Bahia, we have received verbal intelligence from that place to June 11, and papers to the 18th. We do not however from either source obtain a very full knowledge of the state of affairs in the Brazils. The army of Republicans evacuated the city of Pernambuco, as has been before stated, but it was supposed to be still in existence. Many of the leaders however had been taken prisoners, and several then had suffered the punishment of death. Martens and other persons are said to have been taken prisoners, while on accommodating party, and sent to Bahia, where Martens and two others were tried, received sentence of death and were immediately shot. They submitted to the sentence with great goodness and magnanimity. One of them, when brought to the place of execution, addressed the spectators in a bold and impressive manner, telling them that he was about to suffer death for wishing to make them freemen. Several persons were executed, June 15, of whom the following is list, as nearly as we are able to decipher the manuscript in which the names are given us :- Domingos Jose Mez, Miguel Joaquin de Almeda, Bernardo Luis Ferrara Portugal, Jose Luz de Mendonia, and Miguel Jose Perra Caldas.

It was reported that one in four of the Pernambucans, who had taken up arms was to suffer death. Many arrests had been made of suspected persons, in other parts of Brazil, and as there was place for general conspiracy, which was defeated only by the premature disclosure of it at Pernambuco, it was apprehended there would be many executions in all parts of the kingdom.

A fleet consisting of ship of the line, brig, sloop of war, and several transports, having on board 1900 troops, arrived at Bahia May 5, and sailed for Pernambuco June 10. From the sailing of so large force so long after the Royalists had taken possession of Pernambuco, it may be concluded that a considerable republican force remained in arms. II.

Buenos Ayres paper of Nov. 11, received by the brig Cora arrived at this port, contains an official account, communicated by the Governor of the Province of Tucuman, of the capture of the town of Salta on the 15th of April, by the republican Lent Col. Madrid. The prisoners taken were 81, including 5 officers. This advantage was gained with very little loss on the part of the conquerors.

Boston Daily Advertiser.
